\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}. Recent evaluations confirm that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately under compound compression \cite{unicomp-2026}, and that per-dimension safe zones intersect to form a smaller joint safe region \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}, despite evidence that pruning sensitivity depends on representational phase \cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} and that no single sparse attention strategy dominates across generation stages \cite{sparse-frontier-2025}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026}.
Phase-aware methods like ThinKV \cite{thinkv-iclr2026} apply different KV strategies per phase but without considering compound interaction, while importance-based eviction itself faces challenges from greedy bias \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026}, deferred importance \cite{retentivekv-2026}, and temporal dynamics in long generations \cite{lethe-aaai2026}. These methods each optimize a single pruning axis; we characterize the interaction when multiple mechanisms are composed.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

What does compound interaction add beyond single-axis findings? HIES~\cite{hies-2025} characterizes score collapse; ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} introduces phase-aware eviction; \citet{sparse-frontier-2025} document strategy non-dominance across stages. Combining these insights qualitatively predicts phase-dependent compound degradation---but two quantitative patterns cannot be derived from single-axis analyses. First, the severity gradient follows a \emph{strictly monotonic dose-response} across sparsity levels (Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$), not merely a directional trend. Second, in DeepSeek a \emph{strategy ranking crossover} emerges at $s{=}0.25$---importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases and underperforms in low-sparsity phases; Qwen shows consistent importance dominance without crossover, indicating model dependence. We report both the paired median difference $\Delta$ ($0.39 \to 8.48$) as the primary metric and the amplification ratio $G{=}7.5$--$79.8{\times}$ (importance) vs.\ $G \approx 1$ (random) as an auxiliary measure; $G$ is amplified by near-zero $\mathrm{II}_{\textit{high}}$ denominators, but $\Delta$---which involves no ratios---shows the same monotonic gradient (\S\ref{sec:results}).

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems), the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $8.48$ at $s{=}0.30$ (all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$; Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$).
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$); preliminary evidence from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM) suggests the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 but at ${\sim}1/40$ the magnitude and with substantially weaker strategy contrast.
Random eviction develops a detectable but weak phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ ($3$--$17{\times}$ smaller than importance-based where both strategies are significant, $s \geq 0.25$), confirming that the dominant gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We present preliminary correlational evidence for \emph{importance discrimination collapse}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a contributing factor, with the \emph{structural specificity} of importance-based pruning (which selectively removes high-score heads) as a key differentiator from random pruning.

This work is a \textbf{diagnostic study}: we characterize a previously unknown interaction effect rather than proposing a mitigation method. Following the tradition of empirical analysis papers in NLP \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019}, our contribution is establishing and quantifying the phenomenon of phase-modulated compound severity, providing measurement tools and diagnostic findings that inform future method design.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is $3$--$17{\times}$ larger than under random eviction where both strategies show significant phase gradients ($s \geq 0.25$) on MATH-500; the gradient direction is consistent on GSM8K, where importance-based eviction produces significant phase gradients while random eviction does not (\S\ref{sec:cross-benchmark}).\footnote{The full MATH-500 range including non-significant random conditions ($s \leq 0.20$, where random $\Delta$ CIs span zero) extends to $39{\times}$.}
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across two Qwen2-architecture models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), with exploratory evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We provide a \textbf{diagnostic analysis} revealing that aggregate score collapse (Gini) is necessary but not sufficient for severity amplification, pointing to structural specificity of pruned heads as the key differentiator (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Benjamini-Hochberg FDR Correction}
\label{app:bh-fdr}

Table~\ref{tab:bh-fdr} compares Bonferroni ($k{=}4$, per model$\times$strategy family) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all 44 statistical tests. BH-FDR recovers 5 additional significant results beyond Bonferroni, all in low-effect-size conditions (random eviction or cross-training-paradigm random comparisons). All 32 Bonferroni-significant results remain significant under BH-FDR.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bonferroni vs.\ BH-FDR correction summary ($\alpha{=}0.05$, 44 tests). ``BH only'' denotes tests significant under BH-FDR but not Bonferroni.}
\label{tab:bh-fdr}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Category & Bonf.\ sig. & BH-only sig. \\
\midrule
Per-condition Wilcoxon ($k{=}16$) & 10 & 2 \\
Imp vs.\ rand ($k{=}8$) & 8 & 0 \\
Adjacent sparsity ($k{=}12$) & 10 & 1 \\
Cross-paradigm Mann-Whitney ($k{=}8$) & 4 & 2 \\
\midrule
Total ($k{=}44$) & 32 & 5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The 5 BH-only results are: DeepSeek random $s{=}0.25$ and $s{=}0.30$ per-condition Wilcoxon ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.064$/$0.065$, BH $q{=}0.002$), DeepSeek random $s{=}0.25 \to 0.30$ adjacent-sparsity step ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.078$, BH $q{=}0.002$), and cross-training-paradigm random $s{=}0.25$/$s{=}0.30$ Mann-Whitney ($p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.66$/$0.17$, BH $q{=}0.018$/$0.005$). All involve random eviction---the weakest effects---confirming that Bonferroni is conservative but does not miss any importance-based findings.

\label{app:mpl-sensitivity}

Conclusions are robust: all importance-based conditions remain significant at $p_{\text{Bonf}} < 10^{-10}$ across mpl $\in \{5, 10, 20\}$; random conditions maintain the same significance pattern (non-significant at $s \leq 0.20$, significant at $s \geq 0.25$). \section{Segmentation Robustness}
\label{app:seg-robust}

Table~\ref{tab:seg-robust} reports the paired median difference $\Delta$ under tercile, quartile, and quintile segmentation for both models under importance-based eviction. Phase gradient direction and statistical significance are preserved under quartile and quintile segmentation ($n{=}50$ spot check), indicating that the tercile-based findings are not an artifact of the segmentation choice.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Segmentation robustness: median $\Delta$ under tercile ($n{=}496$/$475$), quartile ($n{=}50$ spot check), and quintile ($n{=}50$ spot check) segmentation. Importance-based eviction; all $p_{\text{Bonf}} < 10^{-7}$.}
\label{tab:seg-robust}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccc@{}}
\toprule
Model & $s$ & Tercile & Quartile\; [95\% CI] & Quintile\; [95\% CI] \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{DeepSeek} & 0.15 & 0.391 & 0.491\; $[0.44,\; 0.70]$ & 0.505\; $[0.33,\; 0.71]$ \\
& 0.20 & 1.215 & 1.388\; $[1.05,\; 1.79]$ & 1.197\; $[1.02,\; 1.76]$ \\
& 0.25 & 3.986 & 4.322\; $[3.62,\; 8.06]$ & 4.960\; $[3.80,\; 9.02]$ \\
& 0.30 & 8.481 & 12.930\; $[9.83,\; 19.10]$ & 11.548\; $[10.06,\; 18.51]$ \\
\addlinespace
\multirow{4}{*}{Qwen} & 0.15 & 0.066 & 0.226\; $[0.14,\; 0.27]$ & 0.203\; $[0.13,\; 0.26]$ \\
& 0.20 & 0.307 & 0.561\; $[0.35,\; 0.77]$ & 0.517\; $[0.29,\; 0.75]$ \\
& 0.25 & 1.074 & 1.870\; $[1.05,\; 2.44]$ & 1.801\; $[1.13,\; 2.38]$ \\
& 0.30 & 3.155 & 4.097\; $[2.91,\; 4.94]$ & 4.009\; $[3.28,\; 5.34]$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

The quartile and quintile $\Delta$ values are comparable to or slightly larger than tercile values because finer-grained segmentation isolates more extreme phases (the ``lowest'' quintile captures a more concentrated low-sparsity segment than the lowest tercile). The monotonic dose-response ($\Delta$ increasing with $s$) is preserved across all three segmentation schemes for both models, confirming that the severity gradient is not an artifact of the tercile segmentation choice.


\section{Robustness to Asymmetric Sparsity Allocation}
\label{app:asymmetric-robustness}

Our main experiments use symmetric sparsity ($s_{\text{head}} = s_{\text{KV}} = s$). To verify that the phase-gated severity gradient does not depend on this symmetric assumption, we evaluate two asymmetric configurations at a fixed total sparsity budget equivalent to $s{=}0.25$, using importance-based eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Asymmetric sparsity robustness: per-phase II under two head/KV allocations (DeepSeek, importance-based eviction, $n{=}50$ spot check).}
\label{tab:asymmetric-robust}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
\toprule
Config & $s_{\text{head}}$ & $s_{\text{KV}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{mid}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$ & $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
A (KV-heavy) & 0.20 & 0.30 & 19.51 & 6.05 & 0.38 & $+$19.13 \\
B (head-heavy) & 0.30 & 0.20 & 18.77 & 3.97 & 0.52 & $+$18.25 \\
\addlinespace
Symmetric & 0.25 & 0.25 & 3.97 & --- & 0.02 & $+$3.99 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Both asymmetric configurations produce large positive $\Delta$ ($+19.13$ and $+18.25$), confirming that the phase-gated severity gradient is robust to the head/KV allocation ratio. The KV-heavy configuration (A) exhibits higher mid-phase II ($6.05$ vs.\ $3.97$), suggesting that the KV eviction axis has a stronger impact on intermediate reasoning phases. Both asymmetric $\Delta$ values exceed the symmetric baseline ($3.99$), consistent with one axis operating at $s{=}0.30$---above the symmetric maximum tested---which amplifies overall severity. A systematic investigation of the full asymmetric interaction surface is left for future work.


\section{Outlier Robustness Analysis}
\label{app:outlier-robustness}

The extreme mean/median ratio (up to $97{,}640{:}1$ in individual conditions) reflects heavy-tailed II distributions driven by near-zero denominators in specific problems. We verify robustness via symmetric winsorization at $5\%$ and $10\%$ levels. All median-based statistics---paired median difference $\Delta$, Wilcoxon signed-rank $p$-values, and amplification ratio $G$---are strictly invariant under winsorization, as expected for rank-based estimators. The five core claims---compound exceeds individual, importance exceeds random, monotonic dose-response, $G \gg 1$ for importance, $G \approx 1$ for random---are fully robust. The extreme outlier severity further validates our choice of median-based inference over mean-based alternatives. $G$ values in this robustness analysis follow the ratio-of-medians convention (Table~\ref{tab:profiling-subset}); the primary $G$ definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:gradient}) is similarly invariant as a median of per-problem ratios.

+\section{\texttt{<think>} Token Phase Validation}
+\label{app:think-validation}

+DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B generates explicit \texttt{<think>}...\texttt{</think>} delimiters that demarcate chain-of-thought reasoning from final answers, providing a model-generated ground truth for reasoning phase boundaries. We evaluate whether our attention-sparsity-based phase segmentation (\S\ref{par:phase-segmentation}) recovers these boundaries on GSM8K ($n{=}48$ problems with valid phase assignments).
+\paragraph{Token-level agreement.}

+We binarize each token as ``thinking'' (inside \texttt{<think>}) or ``answer'' (outside) and compare against the sparsity-based low/high phase assignment. Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.887$ (median across problems), indicating near-perfect agreement between the data-driven sparsity proxy and the model's explicit reasoning markers. Of thinking tokens, $57.8\%$ fall in the low-sparsity phase; of answer tokens, $62.7\%$ fall in the high-sparsity phase.
+\paragraph{Boundary proximity.}

+The median distance between the sparsity-based phase boundary and the nearest \texttt{<think>}/\texttt{</think>} delimiter is 1 token, with $81.2\%$ of boundaries falling within 10 tokens. This tight alignment indicates that the attention sparsity transition closely tracks the model's self-identified shift from exploratory reasoning to structured answer generation.
+\paragraph{Phase composition and II correlation.}

+We examine whether the fraction of thinking tokens within each phase correlates with compound severity (II). At the mid-phase level, the thinking-token fraction correlates with II (Spearman $\rho{=}0.49$, $p < 0.001$), consistent with mid-phase segments that contain more reasoning content being more vulnerable to compound sparsity. Low- and high-phase correlations are non-significant, as expected: these phases are compositionally dominated by thinking or answer tokens, respectively, leaving insufficient variance for correlation.
+\paragraph{Scope.}

+This validation is limited to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K ($n{=}48$). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct does not produce explicit reasoning delimiters, precluding the same validation. Phase segmentation is computed on the dense model's attention patterns and is independent of sparsity level, so the agreement statistics are reported once rather than per-$s$.

background.tex:Inspired by ThinKV's phase-aware perspective on reasoning-time compression~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026}, each generated sequence is partitioned into three phases (low-, mid-, high-sparsity) by tercile boundaries of per-position attention sparsity, using a quantile-based segmentation rather than explicit reasoning delimiters (e.g., \texttt{<think>} tokens). Low-sparsity phases correspond to broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning); high-sparsity phases to concentrated attention (structured computation). We note that this segmentation is an \emph{operationalization choice}: attention sparsity serves as a continuous proxy for reasoning phase rather than a theoretically grounded boundary. We validate robustness to segmentation granularity (tercile/quartile/quintile; Appendix~\ref{app:seg-robust}) and minimum phase length (Appendix~\ref{app:mpl-sensitivity}). On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, where explicit \texttt{<think>} markers delineate reasoning, token-level agreement between sparsity-based phases and model-generated boundaries yields Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.887$ ($n{=}48$; Appendix~\ref{app:think-validation}), indicating that the sparsity proxy captures semantically meaningful computational structure. Details in Appendix~\ref{app:formulation-details}.
limitations.tex:The \texttt{<think>} token validation of sparsity-based phase segmentation (\S\ref{sec:background}, Appendix~\ref{app:think-validation}) is limited to a single model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on a single benchmark (GSM8K, $n{=}48$). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct does not generate explicit reasoning markers, precluding the same validation. Whether the high agreement ($\kappa{=}0.887$) generalizes to other models with explicit CoT delimiters, or to non-mathematical reasoning tasks, remains open.
